title: "Exercise 2 — Your first meta-analysis"
format: html
---

## Aim

Fit, visualise and interpret a random-effects meta-analysis.

## 1. Prepare effect sizes

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(metafor)

soil <- read.csv("../data/teaching/soil_carbon.csv")

es <- escalc(
  measure = "ROM",
  m1i = mean_reduced, sd1i = sd_reduced, n1i = n_reduced,
  m2i = mean_control, sd2i = sd_control, n2i = n_control,
  data = soil
)
```

## 2. Fit the model

Fill the blanks.

```{r}
#| eval: false
m <- rma(
  yi = ___,
  vi = ___,
  data = ___,
  method = "___"
)

summary(m)
```

Identify the pooled estimate, 95% CI, $\tau^2$ and $I^2$.

## 3. Back-transform

```{r}
#| eval: false
predict(m, transf = exp)
```

Translate the pooled response ratio into a percentage difference.

## 4. Make a forest plot

```{r}
#| eval: false
forest(
  m,
  slab = paste(es$study_id, es$effect_id, sep = "."),
  atransf = exp,
  xlab = "Response ratio (reduced / conventional)"
)
abline(v = 1, lty = 2)
```

What does the forest plot show that the pooled estimate alone does not?

## 5. Interpretation challenge

Write three sentences that separately communicate:

1. the average effect;
2. uncertainty in that average;
3. variation among effects / implications for a new comparable setting.

Avoid counting how many individual studies are statistically significant.
